questions.prompt: What is a program charter, in the sense this course uses the term?
options: The formal document that authorizes a data governance program to exist, naming its purpose, scope, sponsor, and success criteria
A project plan listing every task the governance team will complete in its first year
A slide deck presented once at a kickoff meeting to generate enthusiasm for the program
A technical specification naming the exact data catalog and tooling the program will use
A policy document stating one specific rule, like a required encryption standard
A meeting agenda template used by the governance council
questions.explain: A program charter is the reference document a governance program points back to whenever someone asks 'who said we're allowed to do this' or 'why are we governing this domain and not that one.' It names purpose, scope, sponsor, objectives, and success criteria — without it, a governance effort is just good intentions any reorg can quietly cancel.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B is the closest wrong answer because a charter and a project plan are easy to confuse — but the lesson explicitly says a charter 'is not a project plan and it is not a slide deck for one meeting.' A charter authorizes the program and defines its scope, sponsor, and success criteria; a project plan is a task list for carrying work out, which is a different document entirely.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 1, the single most common governance program failure isn't bad policy writing or weak tooling — it's scope that tries to cover ________ at once.
questions.explain: A charter that says 'govern all enterprise data' gives the program no way to ever say it succeeded, and no way to prioritize when there's more work than time. The fix is a deliberately phased scope statement naming two or three high-value domains for phase one.

questions.prompt: A governance program's stakeholder register places a frontline data analyst in the 'keep informed' quadrant of the power/interest grid: low power, high interest. Per Lesson 2, what's the right engagement approach for this person?
options: Regular detail, since they care a lot about the outcome but can't individually influence it
Direct, frequent engagement, the same as a sponsor or council member
Periodic, high-level updates only, since their vote doesn't matter
Light-touch awareness, since their interest doesn't translate into power
questions.explain: The power/interest grid's 'keep informed' quadrant (low power, high interest) calls for regular detail — these are often stewards and analysts who need to know what's changing, even though they can't individually approve or block it. 'Manage closely' is for high power/high interest; 'keep satisfied' for high power/low interest; 'monitor' for low power/low interest.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about recruiting stewards, per Lesson 4.
options: A steward is almost always someone with an existing job who takes stewardship on in addition, rarely a brand-new hire
The best data analyst for a domain is often the best steward candidate for it
Time allocation should be left informal, as 'whenever you have a spare hour,' so it doesn't feel bureaucratic
Manager buy-in matters because the steward's actual manager has to agree the time allocation is real
A stewardship program is automatically running the moment a steward role is formally named
questions.explain: Stewardship recruitment needs the right person (deep domain knowledge, often the best analyst for that domain), an explicit stated time allocation rather than 'whenever you have a spare hour,' and manager buy-in that the time is real. Naming a role isn't the same as running a program — most stalled programs named stewardship but never built the recruitment, time, support, and tracking machinery behind it.

questions.prompt: Match each RACI role to what it actually means, per Lesson 5.
right: Told after the fact, with no input beforehand
Does the hands-on work for the activity
Gives input beforehand but has no sign-off authority
Owns the outcome and must sign off — exactly one per activity
questions.explain: Responsible does the hands-on work; Accountable owns the outcome and signs off, with exactly one Accountable per activity, never zero or more than one; Consulted gives input beforehand without veto power; Informed is simply told once the activity is done.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of onboarding someone into a governance role, per Lesson 5, in the correct order.
items: Write the role description, referencing the RACI matrix directly rather than a vague mission statement
Walk the new person through the program charter's scope and why this domain matters
Grant the tools and access the role actually needs — issue tracker, data catalog, policy repository
Pair the new person with whoever held the role before, or a steward in a similar domain, for a shadow period
Make a formal, visible announcement of the new role
questions.explain: Onboarding starts with a written role description tied to the RACI matrix, then context on the charter's scope and why the domain matters, then the actual tools and access, then a shadow period pairing with a predecessor or peer, and finally a formal, visible announcement — a role nobody announced isn't a role anyone else will respect under pressure.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 7, which of these is a 'working,' checkable standard rather than a weak one?
options: Customer PII fields must be encrypted at rest using AES-256 or stronger.
Customer data should be reasonably protected.
Customer data matters to the business and should be handled responsibly.
Teams should try their best to keep customer data safe.
questions.explain: A working standard answers a yes/no question, not a matter of opinion — you can look at a system and check whether PII fields actually use AES-256 at rest. The other three options all use unmeasurable language like 'reasonably,' 'responsibly,' or 'try their best,' which can't be checked against any specific system state.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about how policy, standard, and procedure stack together, per Lesson 7.
options: A policy states what's required and why, in implementation-agnostic terms
A standard is the concrete, checkable rule — a format, threshold, or control — that implements the policy's intent
A procedure gives the step-by-step operational instructions for carrying out what a standard requires
Naming a specific tool or technique inside the policy itself is good practice, since it makes the policy more concrete
A procedure that re-explains why the rule exists is doing its job properly
questions.explain: Policy, standard, and procedure each answer a different question at a different altitude: what/why, exactly what specifically, and how step by step. Naming a specific tool inside a policy is actually a pitfall — that detail belongs in a standard, since the policy then expires the moment the tool changes. A procedure that re-explains the policy's rationale is wasting the reader's time re-litigating something already settled at a higher layer.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 9, if 'critical' and 'medium' severity issues get the same response time in practice, the severity field is ________, not functional.
questions.explain: A severity label only matters if it changes behavior. If every severity level gets treated the same way in practice, the label is decorative rather than functional — it isn't actually driving urgency.

questions.prompt: A governance program needs a one-off decision: a sponsor must decide which of two domains gets a scarce steward headcount this quarter, and several stewards disagree. Per Lesson 10, what guarantees this doesn't turn into a drawn-out fight over who even gets to decide?
options: Naming a single Decider (RAPID) or Approver (DACI) before the disagreement happens
Letting the RACI matrix's existing Accountable role settle it, since RACI already covers one-off contested decisions just as well
Deferring the decision indefinitely until all stewards reach informal consensus
Assigning Accountable to every steward involved, so the decision feels collaborative
questions.explain: RACI is built for recurring activities where the same role plays the same part every time — a genuinely contested, one-off decision needs a sharper tool. Naming the Decider or Approver before the disagreement happens means the fight stays about the actual question, not about who has the authority to decide it.

questions.prompt: Match each DACI role to what it actually does, per Lesson 10.
right: Makes the actual call, the final decision
Runs the process and gathers input
Give input without veto power
Told the outcome after the decision is made
questions.explain: The Driver runs the process and gathers input; the Approver makes the actual final call; Contributors give input but have no veto power; Informed parties are simply told the outcome once it's decided.

questions.prompt: Put these stages of a governance workflow, per Lesson 8, in the correct order.
items: Intake — the request or issue enters the system
Triage / classification — sorting what kind of thing this is and how urgent it is
Routing — getting it to the right person or role using the RACI matrix
Resolution — the actual fix, decision, or approval
Verification — confirming the resolution actually solved the problem
Closure and documentation — recording what happened
questions.explain: Every governance workflow shares this backbone regardless of what's moving through it: intake, triage, routing, resolution, verification, and closure and documentation — the last stage feeding directly into the issue log and metrics Chapter 3 covers.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 11, what makes a number a KPI rather than just a one-off data point?
options: It's tied to a specific decision someone will make, has a named owner accountable for moving it, and is tracked consistently over time
It's any number that appears on a steering committee slide
It's a metric computed once, right before a big meeting, to make the program look good
It's a number that always trends upward regardless of program activity
It's any statistic that IT can pull from a system automatically without manual effort
It's a metric chosen by the data team alone, without input from business stakeholders
questions.explain: A KPI in a governance context is tied to a specific decision, has a named accountable owner, and is tracked consistently over time rather than pulled together once for a slide. That consistency and decision-linkage is what separates a KPI from a one-time data point.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C is the closest wrong answer because the lesson draws exactly this contrast: 'A number computed once for a steering committee meeting is a data point. The same number computed the same way every month, with a trend line behind it, is a KPI.' A one-time number computed to look good before a meeting is explicitly the data-point case, not the KPI case, no matter how favorable it looks.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about leading and lagging indicators, per Lesson 11.
options: A lagging indicator confirms an outcome after it already happened
A leading indicator predicts a problem before it shows up in lagging numbers
A program that only reports lagging indicators is always explaining the past
'Number of policies published' is a strong KPI because it's easy to measure automatically
A mature program only needs lagging indicators, since leading indicators are just guesses
questions.explain: Lagging indicators confirm what already happened; leading indicators predict trouble before it shows up in the lagging numbers, which is exactly why a program needs both — one that only reports lagging indicators is always explaining the past instead of acting ahead of it. 'Number of policies published' is the lesson's own example of a vanity metric: easy to measure, but it doesn't change anyone's next action.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 11, a number computed once for a steering committee meeting is a data point; the same number computed the same way every month, with a trend line behind it, is a ________.
questions.explain: The lesson draws this exact line: consistency over time with a trend line is what turns a one-off number into a KPI — a metric tied to a decision, with a named owner, tracked over time.

questions.prompt: A governed domain shows a 98% data quality pass rate, but almost none of the new reports built against it use the governed source — most analysts still pull from personal spreadsheet extracts. Per Lesson 12's quality/adoption framework, what does this combination actually indicate?
options: People haven't noticed or don't trust the governed data yet — a change-management problem, not a data problem
The program hasn't gotten traction yet and should expect this result early on
People are relying on data that isn't ready, so the quality gap needs urgent fixing
Governance is actually working, since quality is high — adoption will inevitably follow
questions.explain: In the quality/adoption quadrant table, high quality paired with low adoption means people haven't noticed or don't trust the governed data yet — that's specifically a change-management problem (Chapter 4's territory), not evidence the data itself is wrong, and not something that resolves on its own just because quality is high.

questions.prompt: Match each dashboard element to the Lesson 11/12 concept it displays, per Lesson 13.
left: Current value and target shown on a tile
Sparkline trend line on a tile
right: KPI owner
Status (on track / at risk / behind)
KPI's current value and target
Trend direction (leading/lagging)
questions.explain: The value-over-target numbers map to a KPI's current value and target; the sparkline maps to trend direction; the colored pill maps to on-track/at-risk/behind status; and the Owners field maps directly to the KPI owner — the 'who acts on this' piece that keeps a red status from being a dead end.

questions.prompt: Put these parts of an effective executive governance update, per Lesson 15, in the correct order.
items: State the one-line verdict — on track, at risk, or behind — in the first sentence
Give the two or three numbers that justify that verdict, with trend direction
Explain what changed since the last update, and why
State what you need from this group — a decision, approval, or escalation
questions.explain: An executive update opens with the plain verdict rather than burying it after paragraphs of context, immediately backs it with the headline numbers and their trend, explains what changed and why, and closes with a specific ask — everything else belongs in an appendix or the live dashboard, not the main narrative.

questions.prompt: A team does the minimum a new intake workflow requires, but only because it's now mandatory — behavior reverts the moment enforcement slips. Per Lesson 16, which adoption stage is this team actually at?
options: Compliant
Engaged
Unaware
Aware but resistant
questions.explain: Compliant means doing the minimum required, often grudgingly, because it's now mandatory — which is exactly why it's fragile: the moment enforcement slips, behavior reverts. Engaged means internalizing why it matters and doing more than the minimum without being asked, which this team hasn't reached.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the influence/impact stakeholder map, per Lesson 17.
options: The low-influence, high-impact quadrant is usually the largest group, and needs clear training and a visible channel to raise problems
The high-influence, low-impact quadrant needs the same depth of hand-holding as high-influence, high-impact
A stakeholder map drawn once at the start of a rollout can go stale as people change roles
One generic all-hands announcement is sufficient for every quadrant, since the underlying policy is the same
High influence, high impact stakeholders can make or break adoption and need direct, personal attention
questions.explain: Low-influence/high-impact (usually the largest group, the people who actually do the new process day to day) needs clear training and a visible problem-reporting channel. High-influence/high-impact stakeholders can make or break adoption and get the most direct attention — high-influence/low-impact stakeholders need less depth, not the same amount. Maps go stale as roles change, and one generic announcement underserves both the highest-influence and highest-impact groups at once.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 18, a communication plan is not an announcement — it's a ________ set of touches over time, built around the stakeholder map.
questions.explain: The most common rollout failure is treating communication as a single event. A real communication plan is a repeated, varied set of touches over time — a heads-up before launch, a reminder at launch, and a follow-up once people have actually tried the new process.

questions.prompt: A field manager argues a new governance workflow adds a step with no benefit to his team specifically — and it turns out the workflow genuinely doesn't handle his team's edge case well. Per Lesson 20, which root cause of resistance does this actually match?
options: A genuine process gap, not stubbornness — the workflow really doesn't handle this case well
Loss of informal control, since the manager used to decide this himself
A past bad experience with an unrelated governance effort
Extra work with no visible benefit, which just needs more convincing
questions.explain: When a complaint traces back to a real flaw in the new process, treating it as if it just needs more convincing (the 'extra work' root cause) means the resistance never actually resolves — it gets suppressed until it resurfaces elsewhere. The correct response here is routing it back through the governance workflow as a real change request.

questions.prompt: Match each root cause of resistance to its description, per Lesson 20.
left: Extra work with no visible benefit to them
right: The payoff accrues to the organization or someone else, not to them directly
People generalize from a previous poorly run governance or mandate effort
The new workflow doesn't handle a real edge case well
Governance formalizes a decision someone used to make informally
questions.explain: The four root causes are distinct and need different responses: extra work with no personal payoff, generalizing from a past bad rollout, a genuine design flaw in the new process, and the loss of informal decision-making autonomy that governance formalizes away.

questions.prompt: Put these adoption stages, per Lesson 16, in the order a group typically moves through them.
items: Unaware — people don't know the process exists yet, or that it applies to them
Aware but resistant — they see it as extra work or someone else's problem
Compliant — they do the minimum required, often grudgingly
Engaged — they've internalized why it matters and do more than the minimum
questions.explain: Most governance programs get stuck between 'aware but resistant' and 'compliant' — people comply because they have to, not because they've bought in. Moving all the way to 'engaged' requires the communication, training, and resistance-handling work the rest of the chapter covers.

questions.prompt: A new compliance requirement lands, and a quality-tooling initiative needs to move ahead of items already queued on the backlog. Per Lesson 21, what should happen to that initiative's roadmap horizon?
options: It moves from Later toward Next or Now as the new evidence accumulates
It stays in Later, since horizons are only reordered once a year
It's added as a brand-new fourth horizon alongside Now/Next/Later
It's dropped from the roadmap entirely, since roadmaps can't accommodate unplanned work
questions.explain: A sustaining program's roadmap is a backlog re-sorted on a fixed cadence, typically quarterly, as evidence accumulates — a new regulation, a maturity gap, a funding change, or stakeholder turnover can all legitimately move an item from Later into Next or Now ahead of items already queued.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about run-rate budgets and value realization reports, per Lesson 22.
options: A run-rate budget is renewed the same way payroll or software licensing is renewed, not re-pitched from scratch every year
A value realization report needs to promise new value in order to justify the existing budget
A value realization report shows value delivered against the original ask, using the same KPIs and dashboards from Chapter 3
A program whose funding depends entirely on one sponsor's personal relationships is fragile if that sponsor leaves
Once a program converts to a run-rate budget, its value never needs to be reported again
questions.explain: A run-rate budget is an ongoing operating line renewed like any standing cost center. The value realization report doesn't need to promise anything new — proving the existing ask already paid off, using existing KPIs, is the argument for keeping the existing budget. And a program whose funding rode on one sponsor's personal backing is exactly the fragile case Chapter 4's discipline of spreading sponsorship is meant to prevent.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 23, the five generic maturity levels, in order, are ad hoc, developing, defined, managed, and ________.
questions.explain: The five levels describe how deliberate and repeatable a capability has become: ad hoc, developing, defined, managed, and optimized, where the program improves itself and maturity gaps get found and closed proactively.

questions.prompt: Match each maturity dimension to what it's actually assessing, per Lesson 23.
right: Whether the catalog, workflow, and monitoring tools in use actually support the process, or work around gaps in it
How consistently data owners and stewards are assigned and actually doing the work
How much governance is followed because people believe in it versus complied with reluctantly
How documented and consistently followed policies, workflows, and decision rights are
How much KPIs and dashboards actually drive decisions versus sitting unused
questions.explain: Scoring each dimension separately — stewardship, policy and process, measurement, adoption and culture, and tooling — surfaces specific, actionable gaps that a single blended score would hide, such as a program that's Managed on measurement but still Ad hoc on adoption.

questions.prompt: In the Brightfield Agritech case study (Lesson 24), the program's adoption gap outside the original pilot team was eventually closed by which approach?
options: Training run by a respected senior agronomist and communication reframed around growers getting fewer disputed numbers, rather than talking about 'governance'
A new mandatory policy requiring every agronomist to use the workflow, with no changes to communication or training
Escalating every resistant field manager straight to the governance council for enforcement
Replacing the field agronomists' workflow with the finance team's existing tool
questions.explain: Brightfield's adoption gap wasn't fixed with a new policy — it was fixed with Chapter 4's playbook: communication that stopped talking about 'governance' and started talking about growers getting fewer disputed numbers, hands-on training led by a respected senior agronomist instead of the governance team, and a direct, data-backed response to the loudest resistance.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of Lesson 25's program packet, in the order they appear in the nine-step build.
items: Charter and scope — name the domain and what's explicitly out of scope for now
Stakeholders and council — list affected stakeholders and name who chairs the deciding council
One policy — write one real rule the domain needs, and who has decision rights to change it
Two KPIs — name two measurable things tied directly to the original pain this program solves
Roadmap horizon placement — sort three next steps into Now, Next, and Later
questions.explain: The nine-step program packet pulls every chapter into one artifact in this order: charter and scope, stakeholders and council, and stewardship (Chapter 1), then policy and workflow (Chapter 2), then KPIs (Chapter 3), then an adoption risk (Chapter 4), and finally roadmap, funding, and maturity (Chapter 5) — reading the packet back as a whole shows exactly which chapter's fundamentals are still shaky.
